modules.t: The Exam, the ECO & the PMI Mindset
modules.d: How the PMP is built, how it is scored, and the decision logic behind every correct answer.
modules.body:
What you are actually preparing for

The PMP is not a knowledge test. It is a judgment test. Almost every question puts you inside a realistic project situation — a sponsor changing priorities, a team member missing deadlines, a vendor slipping — and asks what an experienced, ethical project manager would do. Several answers will be things a reasonable person might do. Only one is what PMI considers the best professional response at this moment. Candidates who memorise definitions and formulas routinely fail; candidates who internalise the decision logic pass, often comfortably.

The exam is built from PMI's Examination Content Outline (ECO), not directly from the PMBOK® Guide. The ECO organises the exam into three domains — People, Process and Business Environment — each broken into tasks and enablers. The PMBOK® Guide, the Agile Practice Guide and Process Groups: A Practice Guide are reference sources, but the ECO defines what is tested and in what proportion. Roughly half of the questions reflect predictive (plan-driven) delivery and half reflect agile or hybrid approaches, distributed across all three domains rather than isolated in an "agile section".

Verify before you book. PMI periodically revises the ECO, the question count, timing and domain weights. Before scheduling, download the current ECO and the PMP Handbook from pmi.org and treat them as the authority. This course teaches the durable reasoning that survives every revision; your study plan should be calibrated to the current published weights.

Eligibility, application and audit

You need 35 contact hours of project management education (this programme provides them) plus documented experience leading projects: typically 36 months within the last eight years if you hold a four-year degree, or 60 months with a secondary-school diploma. Experience is described per project — objective, your role, and what you did across initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and closing. Write descriptions in PMI's vocabulary, in the first person, with outcomes. Applications are randomly selected for audit; if selected you must produce signed verification from supervisors and copies of education certificates before you can sit the exam. Keep those contacts warm before you apply.

How the exam behaves

Questions are mostly single-best-answer multiple choice, but you will also meet multiple response ("choose two"), matching, hotspot and occasional fill-in-the-blank calculation items. A share of questions are unscored pre-test items you cannot identify, so treat every question as live. There is no published pass mark: PMI uses psychometric analysis and reports performance per domain as Above Target, Target, Below Target or Needs Improvement. The practical implication is that you cannot "bank" one strong domain to rescue a weak one — your plan must lift every domain.

The PMI mindset — the decision logic behind correct answers

When two or three answers look defensible, these principles break the tie. They are not tricks; they describe how a mature project leader behaves.

  • Assess before you act. When something new happens — a risk triggers, a conflict surfaces, a change is requested — the best first move is usually to understand it: review the relevant plan or log, gather facts, analyse impact. Jumping straight to a fix, an escalation or a decision is usually premature.
  • Use the process that already exists. Changes go through integrated change control. Risks go to the risk register and its owners. Issues go to the issue log. Answers that bypass agreed processes — even with good intent — are almost always wrong.
  • Handle it at the lowest appropriate level first. Talk privately with the team member before involving their functional manager. Work the problem with the team before going to the sponsor. Escalate when something is outside your authority or tolerance, not as a first reflex.
  • Be a servant leader. In agile and hybrid contexts especially, the PM removes impediments, coaches, facilitates and protects the team; they do not assign tasks inside a self-organising team or override its estimates.
  • Be proactive and root-cause oriented. Prefer answers that prevent recurrence over answers that only treat the symptom.
  • Deliver value, not just outputs. The project exists to enable benefits. Answers that protect business value and stakeholder outcomes beat answers that protect the plan for its own sake.
  • Act ethically, always. The PMI Code of Ethics — responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty — overrides convenience. Never hide information, never accept improper gifts, never misreport status.
A useful self-check on hard questions: "If my best mentor were watching me make this choice, would they nod — or would they ask why I skipped a step?"

Reading a question like an examiner

Train yourself to read the last sentence first — it tells you what is being asked: the first action, the next action, the best approach, or what the PM should have done. Then read the scenario hunting for three signals: the delivery approach (predictive, agile, hybrid — it changes the right answer), the stage of the project (a problem in initiating is handled differently from the same problem in closing), and what has already been done (if the scenario says the PM already analysed the impact, analysing it again is wrong; the next step is the decision process).

Words such as immediately, always and ignore often mark wrong answers. Answers that sound active but skip analysis ("Replace the team member", "Escalate to the sponsor", "Crash the schedule") are classic distractors. Answers that sound passive but are sometimes correct include "review the risk register" or "meet with the stakeholder to understand their concern" — because understanding precedes action.

Building your personal study plan

A proven rhythm for working professionals is eight to ten weeks at eight to twelve hours per week. Start with a diagnostic to find your weakest domain. Each week, learn one block of content, then immediately drill 40–60 situational questions on it, and — the step most candidates skip — review every question, including the ones you got right, writing down the principle that decided it. From week five onward, add a timed 60-question block weekly; in the last three weeks, sit at least two full-length timed mocks under exam conditions. Aim for consistent scores of 75–80% on quality question banks before booking.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a PMP exam coach. Ask me 8 diagnostic questions about my experience, schedule and confidence across the People, Process and Business Environment domains. Then build me a week-by-week 9-week study plan with weekly hours, topics, number of practice questions, mock-exam dates, and a readiness checkpoint each week.

📚 Glossary

  • ECO: Examination Content Outline — PMI's blueprint of domains, tasks and enablers that defines exam content.
  • Domain: one of the three major areas: People, Process, Business Environment.
  • Situational question: a scenario asking for the best, first or next action.
  • Pre-test item: an unscored question PMI is trialling, indistinguishable from scored items.
  • Contact hour: one hour of structured project management education.

📖 References

  • PMI, PMP Examination Content Outline (current edition, pmi.org).
  • PMI, PMP Certification Handbook.
  • PMI, Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct.
  • PMI, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK® Guide); Agile Practice Guide.

quiz.q: Amina, a Douala-based engineer, plans her PMP study around PMBOK chapters only, arguing the exam is written from the Guide. A mentor reviews her plan. What should the mentor advise her to do first?
opts: Study the process groups in order, since the exam questions follow the predictive lifecycle
Buy a large question bank and let her weakest practice scores decide which chapters to revisit
Keep the PMBOK chapter plan but add the Agile Practice Guide as a second core reference
Download the current Examination Content Outline and map her plan to its domains and tasks
quiz.x: PMI writes items against the ECO's domains and tasks; PMBOK and the practice guides are references. Adding the Agile Practice Guide is a sensible runner-up but still leaves the blueprint undefined.

quiz.q: Kwame applies for the PMP with a four-year degree. He has 30 months of project leadership in the last eight years plus 35 contact hours from a course. Based on the typical requirements, what is his position?
opts: He is short of the typical 36 months and needs more documented experience
He should apply now and add experience while the application is being reviewed for audit
He is eligible if he describes his non-project operational work as project experience
He is eligible because the contact hours compensate for the missing months of experience
quiz.x: With a four-year degree the typical requirement is 36 months in eight years plus 35 contact hours. Contact hours do not substitute for experience, and relabelling operations work would be misrepresentation.

quiz.q: Halfway through his application, Jean-Paul is selected for audit. Two of his former supervisors have moved to other companies in Lagos and Paris. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Ask a current colleague who knows the projects to sign the verification forms in their place
Withdraw the application and reapply next year once his current employer can sign everything
Contact the former supervisors, explain the audit and obtain their signed verification
Request that PMI waive the verification because the supervisors have changed organisations
quiz.x: Audit requires signed verification from the people who supervised the work. A colleague signing instead would misrepresent the record; withdrawing is unnecessary when the real supervisors can be reached.

quiz.q: On a practice question, a sponsor in Nairobi demands an immediate scope addition. Option A says 'escalate to the steering committee', option B says 'analyse the impact of the change'. Using the PMI mindset, why is B usually preferred?
opts: Escalation is reserved for agile projects, while impact analysis belongs to predictive projects
The PM should understand the change first; higher authority may be involved after that
The PM has authority to approve sponsor requests after analysis without involving anyone else
Steering committees are rarely used on the PMP exam, so escalation answers can be eliminated
quiz.x: PMI expects assessment before escalation: analyse, then take the change through control. The PM does not approve changes alone, so the 'PM approves' option misreads authority even though it also analyses first.

quiz.q: Fatou has 230 minutes for 180 questions on a mock exam and is at question 50 after 75 minutes. Which judgment about her pace is most accurate?
opts: She is behind by about two questions, which is within normal variation and needs no change
She is behind; at about 77 seconds per question she should be near question 58 by now
She is on pace, since 75 minutes for 50 questions matches roughly 1 minute 15 seconds each
She is ahead, because the scheduled breaks add time that she has not used yet
quiz.x: 230 minutes / 180 questions is about 77 seconds each, so 75 minutes should cover roughly 58 questions. She is about eight behind, more than ordinary variation.

quiz.q: A candidate meets a 'choose two' item about handling a conflict between two senior developers in a hybrid project. She is confident of one answer and unsure of the second. What is the best exam technique?
opts: Mark the item and skip it until all single-answer items are done
Select the confident option alone, as a wrong second choice cancels it
Select the confident answer, then pick the second option that best fits the same PMI logic
Leave the item unanswered and return to it, since partial answers lose more marks than blanks
quiz.x: There is no penalty for wrong answers, so every item should be answered fully using the PMI logic. Skipping entirely wastes time; the 'confident option alone' approach does not satisfy the item format.

quiz.q: A project manager in Yaoundé discovers that a team member has falsified test results to meet a milestone. On an exam item, which response best reflects PMI's Code of Ethics and the expected sequence?
opts: Discuss it privately with the person, then handle it through the proper organisational channels
Report the issue to the sponsor and let the sponsor decide whether to discuss it with the person
Send a note to the whole team reminding them of honesty standards without naming the individual
Correct the test results personally to protect the project schedule, then coach the team member
quiz.x: PMI's mindset addresses the issue directly with the person and then follows proper channels for an ethical breach. Going straight to the sponsor skips the direct conversation; a general reminder avoids the issue.

quiz.q: Studying in Atlanta, Marcus scores 72% on full mocks but 48% on agile questions. With five weeks left, which adjustment to his plan is most defensible?
opts: Retake the same mocks until he memorises the answers and scores consistently above 85%
Postpone the exam by six months to rebuild his knowledge from the PMBOK Guide again
Spend the time on EVM formulas, since calculations are dependable marks
Target agile and hybrid concepts, then confirm progress on a fresh mock
quiz.x: Roughly half the exam reflects agile or hybrid work, so his weakest area matters most. Repeating known mocks inflates scores without building judgment; postponing is excessive for a targeted gap.

quiz.q: A candidate preparing in Kigali reads a blog claiming the PMP now has 150 questions and three hours. Her course notes say otherwise. What should she do before booking?
opts: Check the current PMP Handbook and ECO on pmi.org and plan from those published figures
Plan for the longer of the two formats so she is prepared regardless of which is right
Trust the most recent blog post, since online sources update faster than training notes
Ask her study group to vote on the figures and plan around the majority view
quiz.x: PMI periodically revises timing, counts and weights, and the Handbook and ECO are authoritative. Planning for the longer format is a cautious runner-up but still does not confirm the real pacing.

quiz.q: A question describes a PM whose team keeps missing sprint commitments and who 'immediately reassigns the work to stronger developers'. Which distractor pattern is this option an example of?
opts: Following the change control process too strictly when the situation is adaptive
Applying a predictive tool such as the WBS to an agile team's commitments
Acting on a people problem before understanding its cause or engaging the team
Escalating to the sponsor before trying anything within the PM's own authority
quiz.x: Reassigning work without investigating the cause skips analysis and team engagement, a classic trap. It is not an escalation, which is a different pattern listed in the course.

modules.t: People I — Leading & Building High-Performing Teams
modules.d: Servant leadership, team development, motivation, conflict and performance.
modules.body:
Why the People domain decides most results

The People domain covers how you lead, build, support and protect a team. It is the most judgment-heavy part of the exam because the "right" answer depends on reading people, context and timing. The ECO tasks include managing conflict, leading a team, supporting team performance, empowering team members, ensuring adequate training, building a team, addressing impediments, negotiating agreements, collaborating with stakeholders, building shared understanding, engaging virtual teams, defining ground rules, mentoring, and promoting performance through emotional intelligence.

Servant leadership in practice

Servant leadership inverts the command pyramid: the leader exists to make the team successful. In practice that means four recurring behaviours. Shield the team from interruptions and scope churn. Remove impediments they cannot remove themselves — access, approvals, missing information. Grow capability through coaching, pairing and training rather than doing the work for them. Create clarity about the vision, priorities and definition of done. On exam questions, the servant-leader answer is usually the one where the PM facilitates the team to solve a problem rather than solving it for them — unless the problem is an organisational impediment the team cannot touch, in which case the PM should act.

Team21 edge: servant leadership is the backbone of Team21's "How Shall We Now Lead?" philosophy. Candidates who already practise it find the People domain far more intuitive — the exam is rewarding the same instincts: humility, stewardship and service that produces results.

Team development: Tuckman and what the PM does at each stage

Bruce Tuckman's model remains the exam's default lens. Forming: people are polite, uncertain, dependent on the leader — the PM provides direction, introductions, roles and a team charter. Storming: friction over approaches and authority — the PM coaches, mediates and reinforces ground rules; this stage is normal, not failure. Norming: agreements form, trust grows — the PM steps back and supports. Performing: the team is interdependent and self-directed — the PM delegates and removes obstacles. Adjourning: work ends — recognise contributions and capture lessons. Teams can regress when membership or goals change, so adding a new member to a performing team often pushes it back toward storming.

The team charter and ground rules

A team charter records values, working agreements, communication norms, decision-making processes, and conflict-handling rules. Its power on the exam: when a dispute arises over "how we work", the first move is often to refer to the team charter or ground rules — and if none exist, to facilitate creating them. Agreements the team writes themselves are far more durable than rules imposed by the PM.

Conflict: sources and techniques

Most project conflict stems from schedules, priorities, and resources — personalities are a less common root cause than people assume. Conflict is not inherently bad; handled well it surfaces better ideas. The five classic techniques:

  • Collaborate / problem-solve — work together to find a solution that satisfies the underlying concerns. Produces lasting win-win; usually the best answer when time allows and the issue matters.
  • Compromise / reconcile — each side gives something up. Useful under time pressure or when parties have equal power; often lose-lose.
  • Smooth / accommodate — emphasise agreement, downplay differences. Preserves relationships temporarily; problem may return.
  • Force / direct — impose a solution. Appropriate in emergencies, safety or ethics issues; damages trust if overused.
  • Withdraw / avoid — postpone or step back. Useful for cooling off or when the issue is trivial; dangerous if the issue is real.

Exam pattern: the PM first encourages the people involved to resolve it themselves, then facilitates privately, and uses formal or forcing measures only when necessary. Conflicts are addressed privately and directly, never in front of the group.

Motivation and emotional intelligence

Expect questions that draw on classic theories. Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policy) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, growth, meaningful work) drive performance. McClelland: people are driven by achievement, affiliation or power to differing degrees — tailor recognition accordingly. Maslow: unmet basic needs crowd out higher motivation. Theory X/Y: assuming people need control (X) versus assuming they seek responsibility (Y) — modern PM practice leans Y. Emotional intelligence — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — is how a PM applies all of this in the moment.

Underperformance: the escalation ladder

When a team member underperforms, the sequence matters. First, talk privately to understand why — skills, unclear expectations, personal circumstances, workload, or tooling. Then address the cause: training, mentoring, clarified expectations, reallocated workload. Document agreements. Involve the functional manager or HR only if the problem persists or exceeds your authority. Removing someone from the team is a last resort and rarely the first correct answer.

Virtual and distributed teams

Distributed teams need deliberate structure: overlap hours, agreed response times, a single source of truth for artefacts, video for relationship-building, explicit norms for asynchronous decisions, and attention to cultural differences in directness and hierarchy. A recurring exam scenario: a remote member is disengaged — the best response is a one-to-one conversation and adjusting the collaboration model, not a reprimand in the group channel.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a PMP People-domain simulator. Present me with 5 realistic team-conflict and underperformance scenarios from predictive, agile and hybrid projects. For each, give 4 plausible options. After I answer, explain the best choice using servant leadership, Tuckman stage and conflict-technique reasoning, and say what the PM should have done earlier to prevent it.

📚 Glossary

  • Servant leadership: leading by serving the team's needs so it can perform.
  • Team charter: the team's agreed values, norms and working rules.
  • Tuckman ladder: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.
  • Hygiene factor: a factor whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence does not motivate.
  • Impediment: anything blocking the team's progress that it cannot resolve alone.

📖 References

  • Tuckman, B. (1965). Developmental sequence in small groups. Psychological Bulletin.
  • Herzberg, F. (1968). One more time: how do you motivate employees? Harvard Business Review.
  • Greenleaf, R. K. (1977). Servant Leadership.
  • PMI, Agile Practice Guide.

quiz.q: Two senior developers at a Lagos fintech publicly disagree on architecture during stand-ups, and the team is in storming. As servant-leader PM, what should you do first?
opts: Ask the team to vote on the two architectures at the next retrospective
Decide the architecture yourself to end the disagreement and restore team velocity
Escalate to the functional manager so they can resolve the authority question
Meet both developers together to explore the concerns behind their positions
quiz.x: Collaborating/problem-solving with the parties addresses the root cause and builds the team. A team vote is a reasonable runner-up but may leave the underlying concerns unexplored and produce winners and losers.

quiz.q: A high-performing team at a Johannesburg bank receives two new members mid-project. Within a week, arguments about working hours resurface. What is the most appropriate PM action?
opts: Escalate the arguments to HR so they can mediate the working-hours dispute formally
Treat it as regression and revisit the charter and ground rules together
Tell the original members that the new joiners must adapt to the existing norms
Remove the two new members until the core team regains its performing behaviour
quiz.x: Adding members often pushes a team back toward storming; revisiting the charter together re-establishes shared agreements. Telling newcomers to adapt sounds efficient but excludes them from the norms they must follow.

quiz.q: A developer in a Dakar team says she cannot finish her tasks because the security office has not granted database access for two weeks. What should the servant-leader PM do?
opts: Reassign her tasks to a developer who already has the required access
Work directly with the security office to remove the access impediment
Raise it at the next retrospective so the whole team can propose solutions
Coach the developer on how to escalate access requests herself more effectively
quiz.x: An organisational impediment the team cannot remove is exactly where the PM should act. Coaching is good practice in general but leaves a two-week block that is beyond her authority.

quiz.q: Your virtual team spans Douala, Toronto and Manila. Members in Manila rarely speak in meetings and decisions seem to favour the Toronto group. What should you do first?
opts: Review working agreements with the team, including meeting rotation and input channels
Replace live meetings with written status reports so time zones no longer matter
Assign a Manila-based team lead to represent the group in decisions on their behalf
Move all meetings to a time that suits the Manila members for the rest of the project
quiz.x: Ground rules and working agreements for virtual teams (rotating times, asynchronous input) address inclusion fairly. Moving all meetings to Manila time shifts the burden to others rather than solving it.

quiz.q: A team member at a US hospital project tells you she is struggling with a new automated testing tool and is falling behind. The tool is standard across the organisation. What is the best response?
opts: Take over her testing tasks temporarily so the sprint commitment is protected
Adjust her assignments away from testing until she learns the tool on her own
Inform her functional manager that her skills are below the role's requirements
Pair her with an experienced colleague and arrange targeted training on the tool
quiz.x: Growing capability through pairing and training is the servant-leader response. Moving her off testing is a defensible runner-up for short-term delivery but does not close the skill gap.

quiz.q: During forming, a newly assembled team for a Cameroon road-maintenance project is polite but unsure who does what. Which PM action best fits this stage?
opts: Step back and let the team self-organise roles so ownership develops naturally
Introduce a performance bonus to encourage healthy competition between members
Give clear direction on goals and roles and facilitate a team charter
Schedule a mediation session to surface any hidden conflicts before they grow
quiz.x: Forming calls for direction, introductions, roles and a charter. Stepping back fits norming or performing; doing it in forming leaves a dependent team without the clarity it needs.

quiz.q: A contractor in your Accra team repeatedly arrives late to stand-ups, breaching an agreed ground rule. Other members complain. What should you do first?
opts: Speak with the contractor privately to understand why, then restate the agreement
Report the lateness in the weekly status report to the sponsor for visibility
Ask the vendor to replace the contractor with someone more reliable
Raise the issue at the next stand-up so the team can enforce its own ground rules
quiz.x: A private conversation first respects the person and seeks the cause. Raising it publicly at stand-up is a runner-up because teams do own ground rules, but naming an individual publicly first can damage trust.

quiz.q: Two functional managers in a Houston manufacturer both claim the same engineer for overlapping weeks, threatening your schedule. Which negotiating approach should you take first?
opts: Accept the shortfall and add a schedule buffer rather than risk the relationships
Escalate immediately to the sponsor, who has the authority to assign the engineer
Use your project's priority ranking to insist the engineer is assigned to you first
Meet both managers to explore interests and seek a mutual arrangement
quiz.x: Seeking a collaborative, interest-based agreement is the first step; escalation is appropriate if that fails. Asserting priority may be legitimate but forces the issue before understanding the other manager's needs.

quiz.q: A team in Kampala has reached performing and self-manages its work well. A new sponsor asks you to start approving every task assignment personally. What is the best response?
opts: Ask the team to decide whether they want the sponsor's new approval process
Comply with the request, since the sponsor has authority over how the project is run
Explain how the team's self-management delivers results and agree on reporting
Approve assignments quietly while letting the team believe it still self-organises
quiz.x: Micromanaging a performing team risks regression; the PM should coach the sponsor and meet their need for visibility through agreed reporting. Simple compliance ignores the PM's role in shaping governance.

quiz.q: Using emotional intelligence, a PM in Paris notices a usually energetic analyst has become withdrawn and short with colleagues for two weeks. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Remind the analyst of the team's ground rules on respectful communication
Check in privately with empathy, ask how she is doing and offer appropriate support
Wait for the next performance review to raise the change in her behaviour formally
Ask her closest colleague on the team what might be causing the change
quiz.x: EI means noticing and responding to people with empathy, privately. Restating ground rules addresses symptoms only; asking a colleague bypasses the person and risks gossip.

facts.t: Year Bruce Tuckman published forming–storming–norming–performing.
facts.more: Adjourning was added with Mary Ann Jensen in 1977. Teams regress when membership or goals change — a new member can push a performing team back to storming.

facts.t: Classic conflict techniques: collaborate, compromise, smooth, force, withdraw.
facts.more: Collaborate is usually best when time allows and the issue matters. Force fits emergencies, safety or ethics. Withdraw is only for cooling off or trivial issues.

facts.t: Herzberg split work factors into hygiene factors and motivators.
facts.more: Pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; achievement, recognition and growth do. A raise will not fix a team that lacks meaningful work.

facts.t: Schedules, priorities and resources — the most common sources of project conflict.
facts.more: Personalities are a less frequent root cause than people assume. Diagnose the structural source before treating a clash as a personality problem.

labs.title: The underperformance ladder
labs.intro: A developer on your Bamenda team keeps missing sprint commitments. Put the PM's actions in the right sequence.

Address the cause with training, mentoring, clearer expectations or rebalanced work

plaibox.title: Simulation: the new member in a performing team
plaibox.intro: You lead a hybrid team building a Mobile Money reconciliation app. Score: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Strong People-domain judgement: you read the Tuckman stage, used the charter and handled conflict privately.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the module: regression after a new member is normal, ground rules come from the team, and conflict is handled privately and directly.

steps.s: A senior engineer joins your performing team. Within a week stand-ups turn tense and two members argue openly.
o: Treat it as expected regression and facilitate a session on how we work
Right — adding a member often pushes a team back to storming; facilitate, do not panic.
Ask the functional manager to reassign the new engineer elsewhere
Removing someone is a last resort and skips every step of the ladder.
Remind everyone the deadline matters more than disagreements
Focus helps, but it ignores the real cause and may push conflict underground.

steps.s: The argument is about code-review rules. There is no team charter.
o: Write the review rules yourself and circulate them
Clear, but imposed rules are far less durable than ones the team writes.
Facilitate the team to agree review rules in a charter
Correct — agreements the team writes themselves are the durable fix.
Let the senior engineer decide, as the most experienced
Hands authority to one person and fuels the conflict.

steps.s: One member criticises the new engineer sharply in the team chat channel.
o: Reply in the channel that this tone is not acceptable here
Public reprimand damages trust; conflict is addressed privately.
Ignore it; a self-organising team should resolve it
Self-organisation does not mean ignoring behaviour that breaks ground rules.
Speak with the member one-to-one and refer to the agreed norms
Private, direct and anchored in the team's own norms — textbook.

steps.s: Two weeks later the team is collaborating well and velocity has recovered.
o: Step back, delegate more and focus on removing blockers
At norming/performing the PM supports and removes obstacles.
Keep running every review personally to prevent a relapse
Micromanaging a performing team undermines its autonomy.
Hold a team lunch and move straight on
Recognition is good, but you also need to adapt your leadership style.

modules.d: Identifying, analysing and engaging stakeholders; communication planning; negotiation and shared understanding.
modules.body:
Stakeholders decide whether projects succeed

Projects rarely fail for purely technical reasons. They fail because a stakeholder was missed, misunderstood, or disengaged until too late. Stakeholder engagement is therefore continuous: identify early and repeatedly, analyse interests and influence, plan engagement strategies, engage through communication and relationship, and monitor whether engagement levels are moving where they need to be.

Identifying stakeholders — early and often

Start in initiating, from the charter, business case, agreements and organisational charts, and continue throughout the project, because new stakeholders emerge as scope, phases and environments change. A regulator, a union representative, or a community group discovered in execution can force costly rework. The stakeholder register records each stakeholder's role, interests, expectations, influence, and current and desired engagement. On the exam, discovering a new stakeholder late usually triggers: add them to the register, analyse them, update the engagement and communication plans — not ignore them because the plan is baselined.

Analysing stakeholders

The power/interest grid is the most-tested tool: high power, high interest — manage closely; high power, low interest — keep satisfied; low power, high interest — keep informed; low power, low interest — monitor. Variants use influence and impact. The salience model classifies stakeholders by power, urgency and legitimacy. The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix records each stakeholder's current (C) and desired (D) engagement across five levels: unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading. The gap between C and D is what your engagement plan must close.

Pattern to remember: a powerful stakeholder who is resistant is your highest-priority engagement risk. The best first action is usually a direct conversation to understand their concerns — not escalation, and not pressing ahead and hoping they come around.

Communication management

The communications management plan specifies what information is shared, with whom, how often, through which channel, in what format, and who is responsible. It is tailored from stakeholder analysis: executives want concise outcomes and decisions needed; teams want detail and context; regulators want evidence. Communication methods fall into three types: interactive (meetings, calls — best for complex or sensitive matters), push (emails, reports — sent to specific recipients), and pull (portals, wikis — recipients access when needed, good for large audiences).

The number of communication channels grows quickly with team size: n(n−1)/2. A team of 10 has 45 channels; adding 5 people makes 15 people and 105 channels — 60 more. This is why growing teams need more structure, not less.

Effective communication also depends on the sender-receiver model: the sender encodes and confirms understanding; the receiver decodes and acknowledges; noise — language, culture, distance, emotion — distorts the message. When a stakeholder "misunderstood" a report, the exam often points to tailoring the message and confirming understanding, not simply resending it.

Information radiators and transparency in agile

Agile teams favour highly visible, low-ceremony communication: task boards, burndown or burnup charts, and cumulative flow diagrams displayed where stakeholders can see them. Sprint reviews invite stakeholders to inspect working increments and give feedback — the most powerful communication tool in agile, because stakeholders see the product rather than read about it.

Negotiation and building shared understanding

Negotiation in projects — with vendors, functional managers, sponsors and customers — should aim for win-win outcomes that preserve relationships for the long term. Principled negotiation separates people from the problem, focuses on interests rather than positions, generates options for mutual gain, and uses objective criteria. Know your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) before you begin; it tells you when to walk away.

Building shared understanding means aligning stakeholders on the vision, success criteria and trade-offs. Tools include kickoff meetings, product vision statements, definitions of done, acceptance criteria, prototypes and demonstrations. When two stakeholders want contradictory things, the PM brings them together, clarifies each underlying interest, ties the discussion to the business case, and, if they still cannot agree, escalates to the sponsor or governance body with a clear analysis — the PM does not secretly pick a winner.

Managing expectations

Most stakeholder dissatisfaction comes from a mismatch between expectation and reality, not from the reality itself. Proactive practices — honest early forecasts, visible risks, early demonstration of increments, and prompt notice of variance with options — prevent the "surprise" that destroys trust. The PMI mindset is unambiguous: never hide bad news. Report status truthfully, early, with a plan.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a stakeholder-analysis coach. I will describe a project. Help me build a stakeholder register with power/interest classification, current vs desired engagement levels (unaware/resistant/neutral/supportive/leading), and a tailored engagement action and communication method for each. Then challenge me with 3 situations where a key stakeholder's engagement drops, and grade my responses.

📚 Glossary

  • Stakeholder register: the living record of stakeholders and their characteristics.
  • Engagement assessment matrix: current versus desired engagement per stakeholder.
  • Communication channels: n(n−1)/2 possible paths between n people.
  • Push / pull / interactive: the three communication method types.
  • BATNA: your best alternative if the negotiation fails.
  • Information radiator: a highly visible display of project status.

📖 References

  • Fisher, R., Ury, W. & Patton, B. Getting to Yes.
  • Mitchell, Agle & Wood (1997). Toward a theory of stakeholder identification and salience. Academy of Management Review.
  • PMI, PMBOK® Guide — Stakeholder performance domain.

quiz.q: Midway through executing a water project in northern Cameroon, you learn that a regional environmental office must approve the borehole sites. They are not in the stakeholder register. What should you do first?
opts: Escalate to the sponsor so that the sponsor contacts the regional environmental office
Continue drilling as planned, because the stakeholder register was baselined at planning
Submit a change request to extend the schedule to allow time for an approval process
Add the office to the register, analyse its interests and influence, then update the plans
quiz.x: A late-discovered stakeholder is added, analysed and planned for. A change request may follow after analysis, which makes it the runner-up, but acting on schedule before understanding the requirement skips a step.

quiz.q: The CFO of a Nairobi insurer has high power but shows little interest in your CRM upgrade. Using the power/interest grid, which engagement approach fits best?
opts: Keep satisfied with concise updates on cost and outcomes and seek input when needed
Keep informed with the full project newsletter and access to the team dashboard
Manage closely with weekly detailed meetings on progress and technical decisions
Monitor with minimal effort, since low interest suggests she will not affect the project
quiz.x: High power, low interest means keep satisfied. Managing closely is a plausible runner-up but overloads a disengaged executive and risks irritating her.

quiz.q: A powerful union representative at a Detroit plant is resistant to your automation project and has started telling workers it will cut jobs. What is the best first action?
opts: Proceed with the rollout and plan to address concerns once workers see the benefits
Meet the representative directly to understand the concerns and how to address them
Ask the plant director to instruct the union to stop discussing the project
Send the union the full benefits case and project schedule to correct the misinformation
quiz.x: A resistant, powerful stakeholder is the top engagement risk; a direct conversation to understand concerns is the first step. Sending documents is push communication and does not engage the underlying fears.

quiz.q: Your engagement assessment matrix shows the Ministry of Health liaison as 'neutral' currently and 'leading' desired. Which conclusion is most accurate?
opts: Neutral is acceptable for government contacts, so the desired level should be lowered
The gap will close naturally as deliverables are completed, so no plan change is needed
The gap is large, so the engagement plan needs specific actions to close it
The liaison should be reclassified as low power to align with current engagement
quiz.x: The C-to-D gap is what the engagement plan must close, and neutral to leading spans two levels. Lowering the target may be valid occasionally but is not the conclusion supported without new analysis.

quiz.q: A Cameroon NGO's donors want summary dashboards, the field team wants detailed task lists, and the auditor wants evidence of spending. Which communication approach is most appropriate?
opts: Tailor content, format and frequency for each group in the communications plan
Send one comprehensive weekly report to everyone so all parties receive the same message
Hold a weekly meeting with all three groups to discuss progress interactively
Post everything on a shared portal and let each group pull what it needs
quiz.x: The communications plan is tailored from stakeholder analysis: executives, teams and auditors need different content. A portal (pull) is a useful component but alone does not meet donors' need for summaries.

quiz.q: You must tell a key client in Abidjan that a critical deliverable will be three weeks late due to a failed integration test. Which method is most appropriate?
opts: An update on the project portal, flagged as high priority for the client
An interactive conversation, followed by a written summary of what was agreed
An email with the revised schedule attached so there is a written record
A formal letter from the sponsor explaining the delay and the recovery plan
quiz.x: Sensitive, complex news calls for interactive communication, with a written record afterwards. An email gives a record but is push communication and lacks the dialogue needed to manage expectations.

quiz.q: A US software client and an Indian vendor are negotiating acceptance criteria. Positions harden over the number of defects allowed at go-live. As PM, how should you guide the negotiation?
opts: Accept the vendor's position to preserve the long-term relationship
Escalate the disagreement to legal so contract terms decide the matter
Focus both sides on interests such as user safety and launch date
Propose splitting the difference so both sides concede the same amount
quiz.x: Interest-based negotiation seeks a win-win by moving from positions to interests. Splitting the difference is a common compromise and plausible runner-up, but it may leave both sides with an inferior criterion.

quiz.q: Your project has 12 stakeholders. A new regulator and two community leaders are added. How many communication channels exist now, and how many were added?
opts: 120 channels now, with 54 added since the three were included
91 channels now, with 25 added since the three were included
105 channels now, with 25 added since the three were included
105 channels now, with 39 added since the three were included
quiz.x: Channels = n(n-1)/2. With 15 people: 105; with 12: 66. 105 - 66 = 39. The 91 figure comes from wrongly using 14 people.

quiz.q: In a salience model review, a community group near a Ghanaian mine has high urgency and legitimacy but little formal power. What does this suggest for engagement?
opts: They can be monitored lightly, since they lack the power to stop the work
They are dependent stakeholders whose claims merit active engagement
They should be managed as the most critical group above the regulator and sponsor
They should be removed from the register until they acquire formal authority
quiz.x: Urgency plus legitimacy without power describes dependent stakeholders who rely on others to advance claims; they merit attention. Treating them as above the regulator overstates their position in the model.

quiz.q: A Paris-based sponsor complains she learns of issues 'from rumours, not from you'. Your plan says she receives a monthly report. What should you do first?
opts: Discuss her information needs with her and update the communications plan
Escalate to the steering committee that the sponsor is not reading the reports
Send her the full weekly team report in addition to the monthly report
Ask the team to stop discussing issues outside formal project meetings
quiz.x: Her needs differ from the plan, so you confirm them and update the plan. Sending more reports is a quick fix but may overload her without matching what she actually wants.

facts.t: Formula for the number of communication channels in a team of n people.
facts.more: 10 people = 45 channels; 15 people = 105. Adding five people adds 60 channels — growing teams need more communication structure, not less.

facts.t: Engagement levels: unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading.
facts.more: The stakeholder engagement assessment matrix records current (C) and desired (D) for each stakeholder. The C–D gap is what the engagement plan must close.

facts.t: Communication methods: interactive, push and pull.
facts.more: Interactive suits complex or sensitive matters, push sends to named recipients, pull lets large audiences help themselves from a portal or wiki.

facts.t: Best alternative to a negotiated agreement — know it before you negotiate.
facts.more: From Fisher, Ury and Patton's Getting to Yes (1981). Your BATNA tells you when to walk away; principled negotiation focuses on interests, not positions.

modules.t: Process I — Scope, Schedule & Cost (with Earned Value)
modules.d: Predictive planning, critical path, estimating, budgets and earned value management.
modules.body:
The predictive planning chain

In predictive delivery, planning flows in a dependable order: collect requirements → define scope → create the work breakdown structure (WBS) → define and sequence activities → estimate durations and costs → develop the schedule and budget → baseline. Each step uses the previous one's outputs, which is why the exam punishes answers that skip steps (for example, estimating cost before the WBS exists).

Scope: requirements, WBS and validation

Requirements are elicited through interviews, workshops, focus groups, prototypes and observation, and traced in a requirements traceability matrix that links each requirement to its business objective, deliverable and test. The scope statement describes deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and assumptions. The WBS decomposes the total scope into deliverable-oriented components; the lowest level is the work package, which can be reliably estimated, assigned and controlled. The 100% rule applies: the WBS contains all the work and only the work. The WBS dictionary describes each element. Together — scope statement, WBS and dictionary — they form the scope baseline.

Two control activities are often confused. Control quality checks deliverables are correct against requirements (internal, by the team). Validate scope is the customer or sponsor formally accepting completed deliverables. Quality control generally happens first; validation follows. Scope creep — uncontrolled additions — is prevented through change control. Gold plating — the team adding extras nobody asked for — is also wrong, even if well-intended, because it adds unapproved cost and risk.

Schedule: dependencies and the critical path

Activities are linked by dependencies: finish-to-start (most common), start-to-start, finish-to-finish, start-to-finish. Dependencies may be mandatory (inherent in the work), discretionary (preferred practice), or external (outside the project's control). Leads accelerate a successor; lags delay it.

The critical path is the longest path through the network and determines the shortest possible project duration; activities on it have zero total float. Total float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project; free float is how long without delaying the next activity. Calculate with a forward pass (earliest start/finish) and backward pass (latest start/finish); float = LS − ES. A project can have more than one critical path, which increases schedule risk.

Compressing the schedule

Crashing adds resources to critical-path activities to shorten them, increasing cost — choose the activities with the lowest cost per unit of time saved. Fast tracking performs activities in parallel that were planned sequentially, increasing risk and potential rework. Compression only helps on the critical path; crashing a non-critical activity wastes money. Resource levelling adjusts the schedule to resource limits and may lengthen the critical path; resource smoothing works within float without changing the end date.

Estimating

Analogous estimating uses a similar past project — fast, less accurate, useful early. Parametric uses a statistical relationship (cost per square metre, hours per unit) — accurate if the model is sound. Bottom-up aggregates work-package estimates — most accurate, most effort. Three-point estimating uses optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P): triangular = (O+M+P)/3; beta/PERT = (O+4M+P)/6, with standard deviation ≈ (P−O)/6. Estimates should be refined as information improves — progressive elaboration — moving from rough order of magnitude (often −25% to +75%) toward definitive estimates.

Budget and reserves

Work-package costs plus contingency reserves (for identified risks — "known-unknowns", controlled by the PM) form the cost baseline. Adding management reserve (for unidentified risks — "unknown-unknowns", controlled by management) gives the total project budget. Using management reserve typically requires a change request because it alters the baseline.

Earned value management

EVM integrates scope, schedule and cost into objective performance measures.

  • PV (planned value): budgeted cost of work scheduled to date. EV (earned value): budgeted cost of work actually completed. AC (actual cost): what the completed work really cost. BAC: total budget.
  • CV = EV − AC (negative = over budget). SV = EV − PV (negative = behind schedule).
  • CPI = EV / AC (below 1 = over budget). SPI = EV / PV (below 1 = behind).
  • EAC = BAC / CPI when current cost performance is expected to continue. Other forms: AC + (BAC − EV) when future work will be at budgeted rate; AC + (BAC − EV)/(CPI × SPI) when both indices affect the remainder.
  • ETC = EAC − AC; VAC = BAC − EAC.
  • TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC): the cost efficiency required on remaining work to finish on budget. Above 1 means harder.
Worked example. BAC = $200,000. At month 4, PV = $100,000, EV = $80,000, AC = $100,000. CV = −$20,000; SV = −$20,000; CPI = 0.80; SPI = 0.80. EAC = 200,000 / 0.8 = $250,000; VAC = −$50,000; ETC = $150,000. TCPI = 120,000 / 100,000 = 1.20 — the team would need to be 20% more efficient than plan on all remaining work to finish on budget, which is rarely realistic. The professional response is to analyse the causes, prepare recovery options and a realistic forecast, and communicate it — not to promise a TCPI of 1.2.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an EVM drill coach. Give me 6 progressively harder earned value scenarios with BAC, PV, EV and AC. For each, ask me to compute CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC, ETC, VAC and TCPI, interpret the project's health in one sentence, and recommend the PM's next action. Check my numbers and reasoning, and show your working for any I get wrong.

📚 Glossary

  • Work package: lowest WBS level, estimable and assignable.
  • Scope baseline: scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary.
  • Critical path: longest path; zero total float.
  • Crashing / fast tracking: compressing with resources / with parallel work.
  • Contingency vs management reserve: identified risks (PM) vs unidentified risks (management).
  • TCPI: efficiency needed on remaining work to meet a target.

📖 References

  • PMI, Practice Standard for Earned Value Management.
  • PMI, Practice Standard for Work Breakdown Structures.
  • PMI, Process Groups: A Practice Guide.

quiz.q: A Douala construction project has BAC $400,000. At month 5, PV is $200,000, EV is $180,000 and AC is $225,000. What are CPI and SPI?
opts: CPI 0.90 and SPI 0.80, so the project is over budget and behind schedule
CPI 0.80 and SPI 1.11, so the project is over budget but ahead of schedule
CPI 1.25 and SPI 1.11, so the project is under budget and ahead of schedule
CPI 0.80 and SPI 0.90, so the project is over budget and behind schedule
quiz.x: CPI = EV/AC = 180/225 = 0.80; SPI = EV/PV = 180/200 = 0.90. Swapping the two (0.90, 0.80) is the common error.

quiz.q: Using the same data (BAC $400,000, EV $180,000, AC $225,000, CPI 0.80), the sponsor asks for the EAC assuming current cost performance continues. What is it?
opts: $445,000, adding remaining planned work to the actual cost
$480,000, dividing the remaining work by the schedule index
$500,000, dividing the budget by the cost performance index
$445,000, adding the cost variance to the original budget
quiz.x: EAC = BAC/CPI = 400,000/0.80 = $500,000 when current performance is expected to continue. $445,000 (AC + BAC - EV) assumes future work goes at plan, a different assumption.

quiz.q: A Nairobi IT team says the cost estimates for the new portal are ready, but the WBS has not yet been created. As PM, what should you do?
opts: Use the estimates for the budget but mark them as low confidence
Accept the estimates and refine them later once the WBS is created
Create the WBS first so estimates can be built from defined work packages
Convert the estimates to a range and baseline the upper value as contingency
quiz.x: Predictive planning flows from scope to WBS to estimates; estimating before work packages exist skips a step. Marking low confidence is a sensible-sounding runner-up but bakes an unfounded number into the baseline.

quiz.q: Your quality team has verified a deliverable meets all requirements. The client in Atlanta has not yet seen it. What is the next step?
opts: Conduct validate scope with the client to obtain formal acceptance
Archive the quality reports and update lessons learned for the phase
Close the work package, since quality control has confirmed compliance
Release the deliverable to production and request client feedback
quiz.x: Control quality checks correctness internally; validate scope is the customer formally accepting. Releasing to production skips acceptance, even though it seeks feedback.

quiz.q: A developer adds an animated dashboard the client never requested, saying 'they will love it, and it took only two days'. What is the most appropriate PM response?
opts: Remove the feature quietly and deduct the two days from the developer's next sprint
Keep the feature, since it adds value at low cost and will improve satisfaction
Present it to the client as a bonus and let them decide whether to keep it
Treat it as gold plating and handle any addition through change control
quiz.x: Gold plating adds unapproved cost and risk; any addition goes through change control. Presenting it to the client sounds collaborative but bypasses the process and normalises the behaviour.

quiz.q: Activity network: A (4 days) then B (6) and C (3) in parallel, both followed by D (5). C's earliest start is day 4. What is C's total float?
opts: 5 days, because D can absorb the difference
3 days, because B is 3 days longer than C
0 days, because C is on the path through D
2 days, because B and C share predecessor A
quiz.x: Critical path A-B-D is 15 days; path A-C-D is 12 days. C can slip 3 days (LS 7 - ES 4) without delaying the project.

quiz.q: A Kigali project is two weeks behind on its critical path. The sponsor forbids extra cost, and two critical activities could partly overlap with acceptable risk. Which technique fits best?
opts: Resource levelling, to smooth workload and recover the schedule
Adding lag between activities so resources are freed for the critical path
Fast tracking, overlapping the two activities while managing rework risk
Crashing, adding resources to the two activities at the lowest cost per day
quiz.x: Fast tracking overlaps activities without direct added cost but raises risk; crashing adds cost, which the sponsor forbids. Levelling usually lengthens the schedule.

quiz.q: A US hospital project reports CPI 1.05 and SPI 0.85 at mid-point, with the critical path behind. Which interpretation best guides action?
opts: The schedule variance will correct itself as more work is completed
The cost underrun proves the project is ahead and needs no recovery
The project is healthy overall, since spending is under control
Work is cost-efficient but behind plan; schedule recovery is needed
quiz.x: CPI above 1 means cost-efficient; SPI 0.85 means less work done than planned. Calling it healthy overall ignores the critical path slippage.

quiz.q: A project has BAC $600,000, EV $300,000 and AC $350,000. The sponsor insists the budget cannot change. What TCPI is needed to finish within BAC?
opts: About 1.20, meaning remaining work must be done far more efficiently
About 0.83, meaning current efficiency is already sufficient to finish
About 1.17, meaning remaining work needs moderately better efficiency
About 0.86, meaning the team can relax cost discipline from here on
quiz.x: TCPI = (BAC - EV)/(BAC - AC) = 300,000/250,000 = 1.20. Current CPI is 0.86, so a jump to 1.20 is demanding. 1.17 is a near miss.

quiz.q: A WBS for a Yaoundé school build has a work package 'Build classrooms' estimated at 14 months and assigned to five teams. What is the most appropriate improvement?
opts: Convert it into a planning package and estimate it after construction begins
Decompose it further until components can be reliably estimated and assigned
Move it to the WBS dictionary and remove it from the WBS structure
Keep it as is, because work packages should mirror the contractor's organisation
quiz.x: Work packages should be small enough to estimate, assign and control. A planning package is a plausible tactic for distant work, but a core current deliverable needs decomposition now.

facts.t: Beta / PERT estimate; standard deviation ≈ (P−O)/6.
facts.more: Triangular uses (O+M+P)/3. PERT weights the most likely value, so it moves less when one pessimistic outlier is extreme.

facts.t: Typical accuracy range of a rough order of magnitude estimate.
facts.more: Estimates narrow toward definitive as information improves — progressive elaboration. Quoting an ROM as a firm budget is a governance error.

facts.t: The WBS rule: all of the work and only the work.
facts.more: Scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary = scope baseline. The lowest level, the work package, must be estimable, assignable and controllable.

facts.t: Efficiency needed to finish on budget when BAC 200k, EV 80k, AC 100k.
facts.more: (200−80)/(200−100) = 1.20: 20% better than plan on all remaining work — rarely realistic. Analyse causes and forecast honestly instead of promising it.

notes.t: ⚠️ CPI below 1: over budget. EAC exceeds BAC — analyse causes before promising recovery.
Behind schedule (SPI < 1). Check whether the slipped work is on the critical path.

modules.d: Agile values, Scrum and Kanban mechanics, estimation, metrics, and tailoring hybrid approaches.
modules.body:
Why roughly half the exam is agile or hybrid

Modern projects increasingly face uncertain requirements, fast-changing markets and technology that is learned by building. Adaptive approaches handle that uncertainty by delivering in short cycles, inspecting real results, and adapting. The exam does not ask whether agile is "better"; it asks whether you can choose and tailor the right approach and behave correctly inside it.

The values and principles that decide answers

The Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan — while still valuing the items on the right. Its twelve principles stress early and continuous delivery of value, welcoming changing requirements, frequent delivery, daily business–developer collaboration, motivated and trusted individuals, face-to-face conversation, working product as the primary measure of progress, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity, self-organising teams, and regular reflection. When an agile question has two plausible answers, the one closer to these principles usually wins.

Scrum mechanics

Scrum has three accountabilities. The product owner maximises value: owns and orders the product backlog, writes or clarifies items, and accepts or rejects increments. The developers create the increment, own the sprint backlog and decide how to do the work. The scrum master is a servant leader who coaches the team and organisation in Scrum, facilitates events on request, and removes impediments. In a hybrid organisation the PM often performs a role close to scrum master plus broader coordination.

Events: the sprint (fixed timebox, typically 1–4 weeks), sprint planning (what and how), the daily scrum (15 minutes, developers inspect progress toward the sprint goal — not a status report to the PM), the sprint review (inspect the increment with stakeholders, adapt the backlog), and the retrospective (inspect how the team works, choose improvements). Artefacts: product backlog, sprint backlog and the increment, each with a commitment — the product goal, the sprint goal and the definition of done.

High-frequency traps. Mid-sprint, a stakeholder asks the team for a new feature → direct them to the product owner, who adds it to the product backlog; the sprint goal is protected. The team cannot finish a story → it returns to the backlog; it is not partially counted. The daily scrum runs long with problem-solving → take detailed discussions offline after the meeting.

Kanban and flow

Kanban visualises work on a board, limits work in progress (WIP), manages flow, makes policies explicit, and improves continuously. WIP limits create a "pull" system: new work starts only when capacity frees up, exposing bottlenecks. Key metrics are lead time (request to delivery), cycle time (work started to delivered) and throughput. A cumulative flow diagram shows bands widening where work is accumulating — a bottleneck signal. Little's Law links them: average cycle time ≈ WIP ÷ throughput, so reducing WIP is the fastest way to shorten cycle time.

Estimating and planning adaptively

Agile teams often estimate relative size in story points using techniques such as planning poker or affinity estimating. Velocity — points completed per iteration — is used by that team to forecast; it must not be compared across teams or used as a productivity target, because points are team-specific and gaming them destroys their forecasting value. Release planning projects velocity ranges against the ordered backlog. User stories follow INVEST (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable) with clear acceptance criteria. A spike is a timeboxed research story to reduce uncertainty before estimating. An MVP delivers the smallest product that tests the key value hypothesis with real users.

Metrics and transparency

Burndown charts show remaining work against time; burnup charts show completed work and total scope separately, so scope changes are visible. A flat burndown mid-sprint signals blocked work — the response is to identify impediments, not to pressure the team. Agile progress is measured by working, accepted increments — not by percent-complete estimates.

Choosing and tailoring the approach

Choose adaptive when requirements are uncertain, feedback is cheap, and value can be delivered incrementally. Choose predictive when requirements are stable, regulation demands upfront design, or the work cannot be usefully split (building a bridge foundation). Hybrid combines them: for example, predictive procurement and infrastructure with agile software development, or a phase-gated governance model with iterative delivery inside phases. Tailoring considers organisational culture, team experience, regulatory constraints, risk, and stakeholder expectations. Transitioning an organisation to agile is change management: start with pilot teams, train, coach, adapt governance and metrics, and expect resistance.

You are an agile coach simulating a hybrid project. Run me through a 3-sprint scenario: each sprint, give me the backlog, team velocity, a mid-sprint disruption and one stakeholder request. Ask what I do as PM/scrum master. Score me against Scrum Guide rules and Agile Manifesto principles, and show me the burnup chart data after each sprint.

📚 Glossary

  • Definition of done: shared quality standard every increment must meet.
  • Velocity: a team's completed points per iteration, for its own forecasting.
  • WIP limit: cap on items in a workflow stage.
  • Cycle time / lead time: start-to-done / request-to-done.
  • Spike: timeboxed exploration to reduce uncertainty.
  • MVP: minimum viable product that tests the core value hypothesis.

  • Beck, K. et al. (2001). Manifesto for Agile Software Development.

quiz.q: Mid-sprint, the marketing director of a Lagos e-commerce firm asks a developer to add a promotional banner before Friday. What should the developer or PM do?
opts: Direct the director to the product owner, who can order it in the product backlog
Discuss it at the daily scrum and let the developers decide whether to take it
Add the banner if the effort is small enough not to threaten the sprint goal
Ask the scrum master to extend the sprint by two days to fit the banner
quiz.x: New work goes through the product owner; the sprint goal is protected. Letting developers decide sounds self-organising but sidesteps the PO's accountability for ordering value.

quiz.q: At sprint review, a story is 90% complete but fails the definition of done because integration tests are missing. What should happen to it?
opts: Count 90% of its story points toward velocity to reflect the work achieved
Extend the sprint by one day so the team can finish the integration tests
Return it to the product backlog for the product owner to re-order
Count it as done and add a follow-up story for the remaining integration tests
quiz.x: Unfinished items are not done and return to the backlog; partial credit distorts velocity. A follow-up story is a common runner-up but breaches the definition of done.

quiz.q: A team's velocity over four sprints is 28, 32, 30 and 30 points. The remaining backlog is 210 points. Roughly how many more sprints should the PO forecast?
opts: About 6.5 sprints, using the highest velocity of 32 points
About 7 sprints, using the average velocity of 30 points
About 8 sprints, adding one sprint of contingency for unknown risks
About 7.5 sprints, using the lowest velocity of 28 points
quiz.x: Average velocity is 120/4 = 30; 210/30 = 7. Using the lowest gives a conservative range bound but is not the central forecast.

quiz.q: In a hybrid project in Johannesburg, the daily scrum has turned into developers reporting status to the PM, who assigns next tasks. What should the PM do?
opts: Ask the product owner to run the daily scrum instead of the project manager
Continue, since the PM needs status information for steering committee reports
Cancel the daily scrum and replace it with a written status update each morning
Coach the team to use the daily scrum to plan toward the sprint goal
quiz.x: The daily scrum is for developers to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and plan; the PM should coach this. Asking the PO to run it repeats the same status-report problem with a different person.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian ministry wants a new citizen-services app. Requirements are uncertain, but the hosting contract and data-protection approvals need fixed milestones. Which approach fits best?
opts: A fully predictive approach, since government projects require baselined scope
A hybrid approach: adaptive for the app, predictive for fixed milestones
A fully adaptive approach, letting the team discover all milestones iteratively
Postpone the project until requirements are stable enough for a predictive plan
quiz.x: Tailoring combines adaptive delivery for uncertain features with predictive control where milestones are fixed. Fully predictive is the runner-up some would pick for government, but it fights the uncertain requirements.

quiz.q: A Kanban team in Toronto has 14 items 'in testing' while testers sit idle waiting for environments. Cycle time is rising. What should the team try first?
opts: Add two more testers so the testing column can be cleared quickly
Move half of the items back to development to rebalance the board
Set and respect WIP limits and swarm on the environment bottleneck
Ask the product owner to stop adding items to the backlog for a month
quiz.x: WIP limits and addressing the real constraint improve flow; adding testers does not help when the bottleneck is environments, not people.

quiz.q: During a retrospective in Accra, the team identifies that unclear stories cause rework. Which outcome best reflects the purpose of the retrospective?
opts: The team agrees a specific improvement, such as earlier story refinement
The scrum master reports the finding to management for a process decision
The product owner promises to write longer stories with more detailed documentation
The PM records the issue in the risk register and closes the retrospective
quiz.x: Retrospectives are for the team to inspect how it works and commit to improvements. A PO promise of longer stories puts the fix on one person and may not address clarity.

quiz.q: A product owner in Nairobi sees that after 6 of 10 planned releases, users already have 85% of the expected value and remaining items are low value. What is the most appropriate decision?
opts: Ask the team to speed up so the remaining releases are completed at lower cost
Transfer the remaining backlog to a vendor so the internal team can move on
Complete all 10 releases, because the plan and budget were approved for the full backlog
Consider stopping or redirecting work, as enough value may be delivered
quiz.x: In agile, the backlog is not a debt; the PO may stop when value is sufficient. Outsourcing the rest is a runner-up that still spends on low-value work.

quiz.q: A burndown chart for a two-week sprint stays flat for the first six days, then drops sharply on days 9 and 10. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
opts: The product owner added work mid-sprint, which offset the team's daily progress
Work is reaching done late, suggesting large stories or hidden blockers
The team is performing well, since all work was completed by the end of the sprint
The chart is misconfigured and should be rebuilt using story points per day
quiz.x: A flat line followed by a cliff typically means work is not reaching done until late, often from large stories or blockers. Scope added mid-sprint usually shows as upward jumps rather than a flat line.

quiz.q: A US insurer's agile team is told by a manager to commit to 40 points per sprint, though velocity has averaged 30. What should the PM advise?
opts: Accept the target, since stretch goals typically raise the team's motivation
Split stories into smaller pieces so the point total reaches 40 each sprint
Use the team's measured velocity for planning and discuss scope or date options
Agree to 40 but plan overtime so the sprint commitment is protected
quiz.x: Velocity is a planning tool, not a target; forcing it breeds inflation and burnout (sustainable pace). Splitting stories to hit 40 is the subtle trap of gaming the measure.

facts.t: The Agile Manifesto has 4 values and 12 principles.
facts.more: Signed in 2001 at Snowbird, Utah. Items on the right (processes, documentation, contracts, plans) are still valued — the left is valued more.

facts.t: Timebox of the daily scrum.
facts.more: It is for developers to inspect progress toward the sprint goal — not a status report to the PM. Detailed problem-solving moves offline afterwards.

facts.t: Scrum accountabilities: product owner, developers, scrum master.
facts.more: The Scrum Guide 2020 replaced the word 'roles' with accountabilities. Each artefact has a commitment: product goal, sprint goal, definition of done.

facts.t: Little's Law: average cycle time ≈ work in progress ÷ throughput.
facts.more: 20 items in progress at 5 per week ≈ 4 weeks per item. Cutting WIP is the fastest lever on cycle time.
